newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Mar 21.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Mar 21.

text.p: New Zealand has offered to help Papua New Guinea negotiate a peace settlement for Bougainville after mob violence erupted for the second day in Port Moresby on Thursday. A guard lopped off a looter's hand with a machete as a mob attacked the supermarket near an army barracks that has become the focus of anti-government dissent over the hiring of mercenaries to attack Bougainville rebels. Page 1.

Opposition leader Helen Clark accused NZ First leader Winston Peters on Thursday of conscripting people's savings "to his idea of trying to buy back the farm". Speaking to Parliament, Clark said the wording of the September national referendum, which, unless amended before the ballot papers are printed, will read "Are you for or against the Retirement Savings Scheme", was preposterous. Page 2.

Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters criticised New Zealand's welfare system on Thursday night as "bloated out of proportion" and a drug that sapped vitality. In a speech to the Festival of Asia dinner in Auckland, Peters praised Asian countries for their approach to social welfare and contrasted their attitudes with New Zealand's. Page 2.

Whangarei MP John Banks has challenged Treasurer Winston Peters "to put up or shut up" over claims that Banks was involved in something untoward in Queensland. The claim surfaced during a parliamentary privileges committee on Wednesday into
allegations that Banks was assaulted by Peters outside Parliament's debating chambers a fortnight ago. Page 2.

Maori Affairs Minister Tau Henare said on Thursday that he did not show Prime Minister Jim Bolger or Treasurer Winston Peters affidavits giving details of shareholdings in companies related to Aotearoa Television Network. He also did not pass the affidavits to the Serious Fraud Office, he told Parliament. "The so-called affidavits were given to me in the strictest of confidence and I have respected that confidence." Page 2.

Retailers expect the months ahead to be "very testing" with little sales growth and further reductions in profit margins likely, according to the ANZ Bank. Many businesses -- and not just exporters -- will find the rest of 1997 a difficult period, ANZ says in its latest Economic Focus. "Indeed, some businesses are likely to experience conditions tougher than in 1996," the report says. Page 8.

Economic growth in the coming financial year will be slower than expected, according to the Institute of Economic Research. The forecasting groups also warn there are risks to the present outlook from a possible current account crisis and potential changes to government policy. In its latest Quarterly Predictions, NZIER has revised its forecast of economic growth in 1997-98 from 3.3 percent to 2.7 percent, but says growth would rise to 4.3 percent in the following year. Page 8.

Insurance payouts on home and contents and motor vehicle policies are continuing to climb, latest Insurance Council figures show. Chief executive David Sargeant said claims had increased in number and cost in proportion to the premium collected. The loss ratio for domestic buildings and contents had risen to 74.15 percent during the year to September 1996, from 73.58 percent in the same period the previous year. Page 8.

Power companies are withholding more than $30 million from national grid operator Trans Power because of disputes over transmission charges. State-owned Trans Power reported a two percent rise in after-tax profit for the six months to December 31 to $46.9 million on Thursday. But at balance date, the company was owed more than $74.2 million in trade receivables, chiefly bills to power companies and generators that remained unpaid. Page 8.

Qantas managing director James Strong has dismissed suggestions that Qantas's $425.6 million sale of its Air New Zealand stake heralded a new era of tougher competition between the two carriers. But he remained coy about the Australian airline's possible entry into the New Zealand domestic market. Commentators in Sydney said Wednesday's announcement that the 112-million share parcel -- the second biggest Air New Zealand shareholding after Brierley Investments -- had been split among a spread of institutions in the United States, Britain, Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia and New Zealand meant the gloves were now off. Page 8.

Average Wellington house prices have risen just 10 percent in the past seven years, the fourth lowest rate of increase for urban centres around the country. But ANZ Bank says in its latest Economic Focus that the Wellington region stands to be one potential beneficiary of the changed economic climate. The heavy rationalisation of the public sector and associated sectors has been the main dampening effect on Wellington during the past seven years. Page 8.
